**A model answer**, for a project created with the answers from [Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d2/p2):

> 1. **`testDir`** names `./tests`, the folder that holds `example.spec.ts`.
> 2. **`projects`** lists `chromium`, `firefox`, and `webkit`. The file also contains entries for mobile browsers, Microsoft Edge, and Google Chrome, but their lines start with `//`, so Playwright ignores them.
> 3. **`reporter`** names `html`, the report that you open in a browser after a run.
> 4. **`baseURL`** is not set. Its line starts with `//`, so it is a comment. You learn what `baseURL` does in [Day 3 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d3/p3).

**What makes a good answer** is that every answer comes from the file itself. A line that starts with `//` is a comment, so the setting on it has no effect. Reading a configuration file carefully is how you find out what a project really does.
3:
**A model answer.** There is no single right plan, but each choice needs a reason.

> **Folders.** I would give each kind of test its own folder from the start, such as `tests/ui` and `tests/api`. Moving files later means changing the configuration, and every teammate has to learn the new layout.
>
> **Browsers.** I would begin with Chromium only. Running every test in three browsers takes three times as long, and early failures are usually mistakes in the tests, not differences between browsers. I would add Firefox and WebKit once the tests are stable.
>
> **GitHub Actions.** Yes. For a team, running the tests automatically on a server each time someone changes the code keeps the tests trustworthy.

**What makes a good answer** is a reason for each choice. The answer "Three browsers, because more is better" states a preference. The answer "Chromium first, because early failures are usually my own mistakes" states a reason.
